OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the anatomy of the fifth metatarsal, identify different fracture zones, and describe how
various fracture locations can predict healing.
Compare the surgical and nonsurgical management of fifth metatarsal fractures, including
proximal and distal fifth metatarsal fractures.
Determine the role of cavovarus foot alignment in the etiology and management of proximal
fifth metatarsal fractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Fifth metatarsal fractures account for at least 25% of all metatarsal fractures.1
The fifth metatarsal has inherent anatomic differences that makes these fractures unique.

Sir Robert Jones described a subset of fifth metatarsal fractures that exhibited a high nonunion
rate because of the inherent blood supply pattern.
Fracture types are categorized according to zones, which may help guide management and
predict union.
Careful attention to the fracture type is essential in treatment selection and optimizing patient
recovery and outcomes.
Cavovarus and metatarsus adductus foot alignment may increase the risk of proximal fifth
metatarsal factors and play a role in healing and refracture.
Distal fifth metatarsal fractures are a distinct type and are associated with different treatment
recommendations.
Zone 1 fractures are the most common type of fifth metatarsal fractures (51%).2
Overall, the incidence of fifth metatarsal fractures peaks in men in their twenties and women
in their fifties and sixties.2
Anatomy, Biomechanics, and Mechanism of Injury
Anatomic differences between the fifth metatarsal and other lesser metatarsals allow for
unique fracture types.
The fifth metatarsal has extrinsic tendinous attachments at its base, with the peroneus brevis
attaching plantarlaterally and the peroneus tertius attaching dorsally.
Little soft-tissue coverage is present along the lateral and plantar foot, and the plantar
aponeurosis has a strong ligamentous attachment at the base.
The base of the fifth metatarsal is divided into three anatomic fracture zones, according to the
blood supply to the bone. The mechanism of injury also may correlate with the fracture type
(Figure 1)

Figure 1 Illustration shows the three types of proximal fifth metatarsal fractures by zone: 1,
tuberosity avulsion; 2, metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (Jones); and 3, diaphyseal stress.
(Adapted with permission from Lawrence SJ, Botte MJ: Jones’ fractures and related fractures of
the proximal fifth metatarsal. Foot Ankle 1993;14[6]:358-365.)
These fractures are best classified on oblique or AP foot radiographs (Figure 1).
Fracture Classification
(Figure 2)
Figure 2 Radiographs demonstrate the Torg classification of proximal fifth metatarsal fractures.
A, Oblique radiograph of a proximal fifth metatarsal demonstrates a type I (ie, avulsion) fracture
extending into the metatarsocuboid joint. B, AP radiograph of a proximal fifth metatarsal
demonstrates an acute type II metaphyseal-diaphyseal (ie, Jones) fracture. C, AP radiograph of a
proximal fifth metatarsal demonstrates an acute type III (ie, diaphyseal) fracture that extends into
zone 3, distal to the vascular watershed of the metaphyseal-diaphyseal region. (Reproduced from
Den Hartog BD: Fracture of the proximal fifth metatarsal. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[7]:458-
464.)
Zone 1 (tuberosity) fractures
Oblique in orientation; proximal to the articulation of the lateral fourth and medial fifth
metatarsal bases.
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Fifth Metatarsal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001172
3/15

Represent an avulsion fracture that may extend into the metatarsocuboid joint
Thought to occur via an inversion force exerted on the peroneus brevis or the lateral band of
the plantar fascia
Zone 2 fractures
Occur approximately 1.5 to 2.5 cm distal to the base of the fifth metatarsal and exit the fifth
metatarsal medially at the intermetatarsal articulation of the lateral fourth metatarsal and
medial fifth metatarsal bases
Referred to as Jones fractures; Sir Robert Jones described the mechanism as an indirect
adduction force applied through the forefoot to a plantarflexed ankle joint3
Transverse or oblique
Occur at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction
May result in prodromal symptoms
Zone 3 fractures (diaphyseal stress fracture)
Transverse and more proximal and diaphyseal, extending distal to the metaphyseal-
diaphyseal region
Also may represent a stress fracture and typically result from overuse or overload, such as in
a cavovarus foot
Can present as acute or chronic
Can be further classified into three subtypes according to age of the fracture
Torg noted fractures with radiographic signs of nonunion or delayed union were less likely to
heal with nonsurgical management; this fracture type can be considered a stress fracture
with prodromal pain before acute fracture, radiographic evidence of stress phenomenon
(intramedullary sclerosis), and no prior management4 (Table 1).
Table 1 Torg Classification of Proximal Fifth Metatarsal Fractures by Radiographic
Appearance
Type
Age of Fracture
Characteristics
I
Acute
Narrow fracture line with no intramedullary sclerosis
II
Delayed union
Widened fracture line with intramedullary sclerosis
III

Surg 2009;17(7):458-464.

Hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy and diabetic neuropathy may predispose patients to
type III fractures by causing inability to sense overloading of the fifth metatarsal bone. These
conditions also can result in a cavovarus foot, which will overload the lateral column of the
foot and increase stress along the proximal fifth metatarsal.
Distal fifth metatarsal fractures
Commonly referred to as dancer’s fractures because of the high prevalence in ballet dancers
Typically occur if the patient rolls over the lateral forefoot with the ankle in plantar flexion,
such as in a ballet dancer en pointe
Fracture morphology usually is a spiral fracture of the distal shaft with varying levels of
displacement that does not extend into the metatarsal head (Figure 3).
Figure 3 AP radiograph demonstrates a fifth metatarsal fracture of the distal shaft. (Courtesy
of Kathryn Lee Williams, MD, Madison, WI.)
Vascular Supply
The blood supply to the proximal fifth metatarsal has been well described as having an
avascular, or watershed, zone in the region of the metaphyseal-diaphyseal bone.5 Fractures
that interrupt the nutrient artery supplying this watershed zone from the distal diaphysis can
further impair healing of fractures in this zone and is thought to explain the high nonunion

rate in patients with this type of fracture, particularly in athletes and in zone 3 fractures
(Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration of the vascular supply to the proximal fifth metatarsal shows the
avascular, or watershed, zone in the metaphyseal-diaphyseal region. (Adapted from Dameron
TB Jr: Fractures of the proximal fifth metatarsal: Selecting the best treatment option. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 1995;3[2]:110-114.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Commonly, history of an inversion mechanism of injury with immediate pain with
weightbearing and often a popping sensation
Zone 3 proximal fifth metatarsal fractures can be considered a stress fracture with prodromal
pain before acute fracture, radiographic evidence of stress phenomenon (intramedullary
sclerosis), and no prior management.6
Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation at the base of the fifth metatarsal
Mild swelling usually present over fracture location
Sensory changes in the lateral forefoot, possibly because of swelling around the sural nerve

9/3/26, 4:09 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001172
6/15

Assessment for cavus foot alignment can be done with partial weight bearing, which usually is
tolerated, or with standing evaluation of the uninjured side, assuming symmetry.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Three radiographic views of the foot, weight bearing if tolerated or non–weight bearing,
usually are adequate for evaluation.
Because the mechanism of injury and presentation of fractures of the base of the fifth
metatarsal are similar to those of distal fibular fractures or anterior process fractures of the
calcaneus, these injuries may be missed if an ankle radiograph is used to evaluate the injury;
to avoid missing this injury, the base of the fifth metatarsal should be carefully evaluated on a
lateral ankle radiograph.
Computed Tomography
CT can be used to assess healing for return to sports activity.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be used to detect early stress reaction/fracture.
Management
The fracture type and patient characteristics drive treatment recommendations.
Zone 1 fractures typically are managed nonsurgically; fractures in zone 2 and zone 3 often are
managed surgically.
Zone 1 Fractures
Typically successfully managed nonsurgically in a walking boot or a stiff-soled shoe for 4 to 8
weeks
Clinical evidence of healing usually is observed after 6 to 8 weeks, whereas radiographic
healing often lags behind.
Surgical management is reserved for painful nonunion or displacement of more than 2 mm at
the metatarsocuboid joint.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001172
7/15

Surgical fixation of a large, displaced fragment usually is accomplished via a small lag screw,
tension wiring, or plate fixation.
Findings of a 2018 study suggested considerably earlier return to work and lower rates of
malunion with initial surgical repair in young adults or athletes; however, no difference was
observed at 1-year follow-up.6
Painful nonunions can occur and typically can be managed via excision of the fragment, if
small, with advancement of the peroneus brevis or open reduction and internal fixation.
Zone 2 Fractures
Many reports of less than acceptable rates of nonunion with these fractures, likely because of
the vascular supply at the location of these fractures
Nonsurgical management of acute, nondisplaced zone 2 fractures requires 6 to 8 weeks of cast
or boot immobilization and non–weight bearing, followed by weight bearing as tolerated in a
walking boot for 4 to 6 weeks.
Callus formation at the fracture site should be evident after 6 to 8 weeks; if no signs of healing
are present, pulsed electromagnetic therapy has been shown to be an effective alternative to
surgical management for delayed unions and nonunions7

Zone 2 Fractures
The rates of nonunion with nonsurgical management range from 7% to 28%. In addition,
the time to union for surgical and nonsurgical management has been reported to be as
long as 12.1 weeks and 21.2 weeks, respectively.8 Therefore, surgical management is a
reasonable treatment option for acute zone 2 fractures in athletes or informed patients
who would prefer surgical treatment rather than the risk of nonunion and accept the
risks associated with surgical treatment.9
Zone 3 Fractures
Proximal diaphyseal stress fractures may show signs of delayed union or nonunion as
indicated by the presence of intramedullary sclerosis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:09 PM
AAOS | Fifth Metatarsal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001172
8/15

Because of increased rates of nonunion, surgical treatment typically is offered to athletes,
patients with a cavovarus foot, and patients with a Torg type II or type III fracture.
Distal Fifth Metatarsal Fractures
Nonsurgical management via weight bearing as tolerated in a walking boot or cast is
considered acceptable for most of these fractures.
Angulation greater than 10° or displacement of 3 to 4 mm has been suggested as an indication
for surgical management.10

Distal Fifth Metatarsal Fractures
Excellent results can be achieved with nonsurgical management. O’Malley et al11
reported on 35 professional ballet dancers with an mean return to pain-free weight
bearing at 6.1 weeks and return to performance at 19 weeks, reporting one delayed
union at 7 months and one refracture at 2 months.
Surgical Management of Zones 2 and Zone 3 Fractures
(Video 1)

Video 1 Den Hartog BD: Video. Fracture of the Proximal Fifth Metatarsal. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2009;17(7):458-464.
The most common surgical treatment option consists of intramedullary screw fixation with
reaming/drilling of the canal.
Compression at the fracture site typically is achieved with the use of a partially threaded
screw.
Bone grafting in the form of autograft or allograft or biologic supplementation (ie, bone
marrow aspirate) may aid in healing of nonunion or refracture.
Nonunions or refractures typically are managed via intramedullary screw fixation.
Corticocancellous inlay bone grafting also has been proposed as a treatment option, usually in
combination with internal fixation.9
Plantarlateral plating has been proposed as an alternative to intramedullary screw fixation for
acute and recurrent fractures.
Biomechanical studies on plantarlateral plating have suggested greater cycles to failure and
peak load before failure and less gap width compared with intramedullary screw fixation.13
Clinical studies on plantar plating for acute fractures have demonstrated radiographic union
at a mean follow-up of 9.3 weeks but with a 10.5% refracture rate. This technique can be
used for refractures and nonunions, but it is not commonly used for acute fractures.

Surgical Management of Zones 2 and Zone 3 Fractures
The optimal length and type of screw are subjects of debate, and cortical purchase,
bending strength, pullout strength, and screw design have been studied. The consensus
is that the largest-diameter solid screw that fits snugly within the canal with threads
across the fracture and engaging the diaphysis distal to fracture should be used. The
most common screw sizes include 4.5 mm, 5.5 mm, and 6.5 mm.12
Surgical Technique for Zone 2 and Zone 3 Fractures (Video 1)
Outpatient setting using an ankle block with general or spinal anesthesia
Positioned in a semilateral position with beanbag to ensure access to the lateral hindfoot for
placement of guidewire and screw
Fluoroscopy is necessary; mini or large fluoroscopy can be used.
Most surgeons use a guidewire cannulated system for drilling/reaming and tapping and then
place a solid screw; however, use of a guidewire and cannulated drilling are not essential.
Accurate placement of the guidewire or accurate drilling if no guidewire is used is essential;
the guidewire or drill should enter the fifth metatarsal canal in the high and inside position
(Figure 5).
Figure 5 Photographs show guidewire positioning during surgical management of proximal
fifth metatarsal fractures. A, Photograph shows a bone model of a foot with a black dot
indicating the correct entry point for the guidewire on the styloid process of the fifth
metatarsal. B, Intraoperative photograph shows alignment of the guidewire inserted into the

11/15

base of the fifth metatarsal. (Reproduced from Den Hartog BD: Fracture of the proximal fifth
metatarsal. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[7]:458-464.)
The guidewire or drill should be advanced up to, but not beyond, the natural curve of the fifth
metatarsal to avoid distal fracture with placement of a screw that is too long.
A cannulated drill bit is then used to drill the canal to the expected screw length if a guidewire
is used.
Solid or cannulated taps are used to cut the channel for threads and assess for screw size to
ensure adequate endosteal bite.
A solid screw of appropriate length (threads should be past the fracture but avoiding
deformation of the metatarsal or breach of the cortex) is then placed.
Burying the screw head may prevent impingement on the cuboid.
Complications
Rates of refracture and nonunion of Jones fractures as high as 50% have been reported,
usually because of return to sport in season. Nonunions and refractures typically are managed
via removal of the existing screw and takedown of the fracture site. The medullary canal is
then drilled. Autograft often is used for bone grafting. Other biologic supplementation options,
such as bone marrow aspirate, also may be used.14 A screw that is different (larger diameter,
longer, shorter, screw type, composition) than the original screw is then placed.
Sural nerve irritation
Painful, prominent screw head
The Role of Cavovarus Foot
A varus hindfoot or varus heel, metatarsus adductus, or a plantarflexed first ray has been
shown to affect healing times and may be associated with a higher risk of fractures in zone 2
and zone 3.15
In patients with a nonunion or recurrent zone 2 or zone 3 fracture, surgeons must determine if
mechanical reasons for the delay in healing or refracture exist and manage those surgically at
the time of revision surgery.

The Role of Cavovarus Foot

Additional procedures that may be necessary to correct an alignment problem should be
assessed via a clinical and radiographic examination, including the Coleman block test,
to determine the presence of fixed hindfoot varus, a plantarflexed first ray and/or
metatarsus adductus. Additional procedures, such as a lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy,
shortening of the lateral column, a dorsiflexion first ray osteotomy, or peroneus longus
to brevis transfer, can be performed simultaneously.
